#8205. Three Ground Rules for Getting Outside

Getting outside is for everyone. That’s what Sierra is all about, finding top active and outdoor brands at prices that make it accessible to try a bunch of new adventures. That’s the spirit behind Sierra in the Sierras, in which Dylan Efron (Emmy-winning co-producer of Netflix’s Down to Earth with Zac Efron) hits the trail with a friend to try something completely new.

With gear and apparel from Sierra and guidance from Outside editors, in episode one Dylan explores the Sierra Nevada with Danielle Fishel, Boy Meets World icon and Dancing With the Stars co-star. Along with new adventures, they learn some fundamental principles for having fun outside. Ones you can use yourself.

Whether it’s your first hike or just your first hike today, no one likes to be uncomfortable. The right gear helps. If you’re like Danielle, a self-proclaimed “indoor person,” or simply trying a new activity, you’ll want to focus on comfort and versatility above all else. The aim is to A) feel good while enjoying your new hobby and B) have the freedom to explore further as you progress. The gear choices at Sierra make this easy, thanks to a combo of trusted brands, great prices, and an ever evolving inventory of fresh finds in-store and online.

Like most things in life, getting outside is better with friends. In the first episode of Sierra in the Sierras, Dylan recruits Outside’s Climbing Editor, Anthony Walsh, to give Danielle a lesson in bouldering. And that’s just the start. Next up is slacklining and then a highlining adventure.

If you’re nervous about trying a new sport, having a friend or guide to show you the ropes (literally or figuratively) can make a big difference. But the most important thing is trying something new—it can be just as fun to be complete beginners together.

Dylan and Danielle got the chance to explore the stunning terrain in the Sierra Nevada around Lake Tahoe, but you don’t have to wait for your next big trip to take an adventure outside. Wherever you live, there are more natural playgrounds in your area than you think. Use apps like Trailforks and Gaia GPS to plan your next outing, and discover the outdoors in your own backyard.

The world says to go harder, faster, stronger—but Sierra says, “go however you want.” From hiking up mountains to strolling down the block, Sierra loves it all. Whether you’re athletic or more athletish, Sierra has tons of active & outdoor essentials like top-brand gear, footwear, apparel & more for everything you’re into, all at unexpectedly low prices.

#8204. We’d Rather Spend the Holidays in These 7 Gorgeous Ski Town Rentals

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Reflect in the Wild @ Lions Lair, a mirrored Catskills hideaway near Hunter Mountain. (Photo: Courtesy of Airbnb)

I’ve planned most of my ski trips around one thing: the skiing. How’s the terrain? What’s the vert? How deep is the base? When’s the next storm?

Where I’m sleeping has generally been a secondary consideration. Give me a comfortable bed, a place to dry my gear, and a clean bathroom, and I’m happy.

But this holiday season, I’m dreaming bigger. What if, instead of the usual marathon of cooking, cleaning, and navigating family drama, we packed up our skis, gathered our favorite people, and disappeared into the mountains for a few days?

Of course, if I’m going to convince everyone to trade their usual holiday traditions for a ski trip, a cramped motel room and a communal boot dryer probably won’t cut it.

A gorgeous cabin with a roaring fireplace, a proper kitchen for holiday dinners, and a hot tub waiting after last chair? Now we’re talking.

Apparently, I’m not the only one who likes the idea.

According to Airbnb’s latest winter travel report, travelers are increasingly looking to smaller mountain towns for their holiday getaways. Searches for holiday stays in Hunter, New York, are up 37 percent year over year, while ski destinations like Brian Head, Utah, and Mammoth Lakes, California, also made the company’s list of trending winter escapes.

And with Airbnb’s new checkout rules, which generally prohibit hosts from requiring guests to strip beds, start laundry, or wash and put away dishes for bookings made on or after November 20, what’s not to love? Sorry, family and friends, the same rules do not apply at Chalet de Shafer. Here’s a sponge.

From a sprawling Mammoth chalet that sleeps 12 to a romantic mirrored hideaway in the Catskills, these seven properties offer a compelling alternative to the usual holiday routine: beautiful mountain settings, plenty of character, inspiration to make a few new traditions, and, most importantly, nearby skiing.

Some ski trips are easy; others require a group chat, a shared grocery list, and a spreadsheet. This five-bedroom Mammoth Lakes townhouse was made for the latter.

Located near Canyon Lodge, the spacious retreat sleeps 12 and offers easy access to one of the West’s most impressive ski mountains. The townhouse puts skiers near several lifts, with access to beginner terrain, intermediate cruisers, and connections to Mammoth’s more challenging slopes. There’s also a free gondola connecting Canyon Lodge to the Village, making dinner and après plans a lot easier.

I’ve been on enough group ski trips to know that getting 12 people out the door at the same time is an unachievable goal. That’s why staying within walking distance of multiple lifts accessing Mammoth’s sprawling terrain is such a gift. Everyone can ski on their own schedule, and nobody has to organize a carpool.

Mammoth ranked No. 7 in the West in SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide and landed in the Top 10 for snow, grooming, and terrain variety. With more than 3,500 acres of skiable terrain, 3,100 feet of vertical, and a summit elevation above 11,000 feet, it’s the kind of mountain that can keep even the most ambitious skiers occupied for days.

Inside the townhouse, you’ll find a wood-burning fireplace, private steam room, arcade table, and a well-equipped kitchen designed to feed a crowd. There’s ski and gear storage, too, which anyone who has shared a vacation rental with 11 other skiers will appreciate.

And because the Canyon Lodge lifts are within walking distance, you can leave the cars parked and focus on the important stuff, like who forgot to buy coffee and whose turn it is to make breakfast.

New Yorkers don’t have to travel far to find a proper ski weekend. Hunter Mountain, about 2.5 hours from the city, offers 1,600 feet of vertical and some of the most substantial lift-served skiing in the Catskills. And while Western skiers might turn their noses up at skiing in New York, anyone who’s spent time on the East Coast knows there’s a particular satisfaction in making the most of whatever winter throws at you. Hunter’s extensive snowmaking helps with that.

And just down the road is an architecturally stunning 225-square-foot mirrored tiny home that practically disappears into the surrounding forest. There’s a private wraparound deck with a hot tub, hammock, and outdoor fireplace, plus access to an all-glass sauna. It’s the kind of place that makes a romantic ski weekend feel considerably more romantic.

And if you’re a true New Yorker without a car, take a tip from my friend Abby and take the $59 round-trip ski bus from Manhattan to Hunter Mountain. You’ll still need to figure out transportation between the mountain and the cabin, but it’s a pretty compelling alternative to renting a car for the weekend. Check the bus schedule before planning an overnight stay.

This ski-town rental has one amenity that immediately caught our attention: a private sauna overlooking a Vermont river.

Located along the Brewster River near Smugglers’ Notch, this two-bedroom cottage is surrounded by 20 acres of mountain scenery. Large windows frame the water, while a wood-burning fire pit and sauna make post-ski recovery a major draw.

The fully equipped kitchen and riverside dining area are ideal for slow mornings, though there’s plenty of reason to head out early. Just a short drive away, Smugglers’ Notch Resort spreads across three mountains, with 78 trails and plenty of tree skiing.

Smugglers’ Notch has a reputation as a family resort (it earned the No. 2 spot for family friendliness in our 2027 Resort Guide), which might lead you to imagine an endless procession of pizza wedges and children in matching ski-school vests. But over on Madonna and Sterling, the mountain has some legitimately challenging terrain, including steep trails and tree skiing that demand your full attention.

Smuggs ranked No. 11 in the East in SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide and earned the No. 3 spot for value and No. 5 for terrain variety. Not bad for a mountain that still feels refreshingly old-school. In other words, you can spend the day skiing some legitimately challenging terrain and the evening recovering in a sauna with a view, with absolutely no obligation to do anything productive.

One thing to know: The hosts require four-wheel or all-wheel drive for winter access, and Route 108 through Smugglers’ Notch Pass closes seasonally.

Some ski trip lodging is designed for little more than getting some sleep between ski days. Others feel like the main event.

The Cabin at Bear River, a 560-square-foot retreat tucked into 3.5 wooded acres near Sunday River, falls firmly into the second category.

The fireplace, radiant-heated floors, and well-equipped kitchen, complete with a fondue pot and KitchenAid mixer, make a compelling case for a particularly civilized après experience.

When you’re ready to ski off that Gruyère, Sunday River is just down the road. Spanning eight interconnected peaks and 884 skiable acres, the Maine resort offers everything from long groomers to challenging steeps. Expert skiers can test themselves on White Heat, one of the East’s famously steep double-black-diamond runs, while intermediates will find plenty to explore across the mountain.

Sunday River ranked No. 9 in the East in SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide and earned top-10 honors for grooming, lifts, and terrain variety.

Back at the cabin, there’s a private sauna and outdoor hot tub waiting. Call it recovery if you want. Personally, I don’t need a sports scientist to justify cranking those jets all the way up.

Utah’s ski reputation has been built largely on the Cottonwood Canyons, and for good reason. But there’s a whole other ski experience waiting four hours south of Salt Lake City, where the mountains look nothing like the Wasatch, the base elevation is a lofty 9,600 feet, and you don’t have to spend your morning sitting in the red snake of traffic wondering whether everyone else in the state also called in sick.

Brian Head Resort is one of Utah’s highest-elevation ski resorts. Its two mountains, Giant Steps and Navajo, offer 72 trails and 1,320 feet of vertical. Navajo is a good place for beginners to get their ski legs, while Giant Steps has more challenging terrain, including intermediate and expert runs and terrain parks.

The surrounding landscape is a world away from the Wasatch, too. Think high-desert scenery, red-rock country, and the chance to tack on a visit to nearby Cedar Breaks National Monument.

And tucked among the trees, just a short drive from the lifts, is this striking Scandinavian-inspired chalet that I think I might actually take off this list so I can have it all to myself. (Quickly Googles “squatters’ rights in Utah.”)

Inside, expansive windows let in plenty of natural light, while the clean, modern interiors make an excellent case for doing very little after skiing beyond enjoying the private hot tub and fire pit right outside.

With room for eight guests, it’s a great option for a group trip, especially if your friends appreciate a good at-home après setup as much as fresh snow.

If your ideal winter vacation includes a wood-burning fireplace, a good book, and excellent New England skiing, let us introduce The Conscious Cabin.

This renovated 777-square-foot log cabin sits on three wooded acres in New Hampshire’s White Mountains, less than 10 minutes from downtown North Conway.

Inside, exposed timber and cozy furnishings deliver exactly the kind of atmosphere you’d hope for from a New England cabin. Outside, there’s a spacious backyard with a fire pit, gazebo, and a short trail leading to a brook.

Nearby Cranmore Mountain, just outside downtown North Conway, offers 1,200 feet of vertical and 60 trails, and is particularly well suited to families and skiers who appreciate cruising groomers. For more challenging terrain, head to Attitash, where two peaks offer more than 300 skiable acres, including classic New England trails, glades, and steeper runs.

Both resorts made SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide, ranking No. 17 and No. 19 in the East, respectively. Cranmore also took the top spot for lodging and ranked No. 4 for dining, making North Conway an especially appealing base for a winter getaway.

After all, this charming cabin is considerably more appealing than spending the holidays sleeping on your aunt’s pullout couch in the basement.

If your ideal ski vacation includes a little European charm without the transatlantic flight, Mont-Tremblant makes a pretty convincing case.

The Québec resort is known for its colorful pedestrian village, lively après scene, and some of the most substantial lift-served skiing in Eastern Canada.

With more than 100 trails spread across four mountain faces, 763 skiable acres, and 2,116 feet of vertical, Tremblant has enough terrain to keep everyone from beginners to expert skiers entertained. Its extensive snowmaking system is another welcome advantage for early-season trips.

Perched on the mountainside, Horizon 115-204 is a modern three-bedroom condo with ski-in/ski-out access, so you can go from breakfast to the slopes without a complicated transportation plan.

Inside, there’s a gas fireplace, a fully equipped kitchen, and enough room for eight guests. A balcony offers mountain air and space for a post-ski drink, while an on-site hot tub gives you another great reason to get out of your ski boots quickly.

And if you’re not quite ready to call it a night, the resort’s pedestrian village is accessible by shuttle, with restaurants, bars, and enough après activity to keep the evening going.

#8203. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

Posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

When Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

When he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

“The rope would drop us off here,” he says. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

“Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

Mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he says, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”

In a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees says. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

“It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”

Scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

As the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

While sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he says. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”

Since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he says. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque says that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I said, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”

Inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque says, “but mountain sports have not.”

While private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque says the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he says. “We have the potential.”

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an important mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he says.

Through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily said yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he says.

#8202. How a 20-Year-Old Texas Climber Lost His Life on the Matterhorn

Kieran Liner, a 20-year-old climber based in Austin, TX, died in an accident on the Matterhorn in October. (Photo: Courtesy Precenia Newman)

A 20-year-old climber named Kieran Liner from Austin, Texas, died on October 27 after falling from the Matterhorn’s Hörnli Ridge. He was climbing with his friend Eli Hawkins.

Valais Cantonal Police said the two climbers were ascending shortly after 6 a.m. when rocks fell near them at about 11,500 feet. Hawkins lost sight of Liner and immediately called for help. An Air Zermatt helicopter responded. Rescuers found Liner below the route and pronounced him dead at the scene.

Prosecutors opened an investigation to determine the precise circumstances of the fall. The initial police statement reported rockfall nearby, but didn’t specify exactly how Liner fell or died.

Hawkins, who says he met Liner in Austin around five years ago, called him his “best bud” and his climbing partner. “It is what it is,” Hawkins told Climbing. “He died doing what he loved.”

Originally from Pensacola, Florida, Liner had lived in Austin since 2020. According to Hawkins, Liner liked Modest Mouse, IPAs, and American Spirit Blues. But what he loved most, Hawkins wrote, was climbing in the mountains.

In an obituary shared last week, Liner’s sister Precenia Newman remembered her younger brother as a skateboarder, golfer, and alpinist—someone who brought the same enthusiasm to everything he pursued. “He approached everything in life with 150% of himself,” Newman wrote.

Newman described a close circle of friends who had become family through shared adventures and everyday life. Among them was Hawkins, whose friendship and life as Liner’s roommate she singled out as especially meaningful. She also remembered the love surrounding Liner from his parents, Justine Hamel and Nick Liner, as well as his siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, nieces, and nephews. Newman has organized a fundraiser to bring him home so the family can celebrate his life in Pensacola and Austin.

While Hawkins grew up climbing as a kid with his father and uncle, Liner got into the sport later in life, but it quickly became his passion. Hawkins said the two of them had strong mentors, including Hawkins’s dad Stephen, Ben Darce, and his uncle Bryan Hawkins who owns a climbing gym in Everett, Washington. “He was fearless,” Hawkins said of Liner. “I was fearless—still am. I’m going to keep climbing for him. We just climbed hard and partied hard.”

This past July, Liner had started an Instagram account called @mountkieran dedicated primarily to climbing and mountaineering content. His first reel captured climbing Mt. Rainier. Most of his content leaned humorous, with jokes about “Conrad Anger” and poking fun at himself as an “Austin influencer” while board climbing.

But occasionally, Liner shared more serious content, like footage of ascending a steep snow pitch with a quote from Reinhold Messner: “To go on an adventure, you need difficulties, you need danger. If death were not a possibility, coming out would be nothing.”

Generally considered the most popular and easiest route by which to ascend the Matterhorn, the Hörnli Ridge rises roughly 4,000 vertical feet from the Hörnli Hut to the 14,692-foot summit. Rated AD (“fairly difficult”) on the alpine scale, the route combines sustained exposed scrambling with technical rock climbing rated around 5.4. In general, parties take four to five hours for the ascent, plus another five to six hours for the descent, which involves downclimbing and rappelling much of the same terrain.

Fixed ropes assist climbers on certain sections, but parties also bring their own ropes. Snow and ice can be encountered near the summit, requiring crampons and an ice axe. The technical grade captures only part of the challenge of navigating and descending that exposed terrain in mountaineering boots.

To learn more about the Hörnli Ridge where Liner’s accident took place, I reached out to my friend Steph Abegg, who claimed the fastest known time by a woman on the route this past summer.

In 1985, Abegg’s dad soloed the Matterhorn in a T-shirt. Twenty years later, when Abegg and her sister were in Zermatt and decided to climb it, that was the image they held in their minds. Their dad was an experienced climber, and he’d enjoyed ideal conditions on his ascent.

Accordingly, the Abegg sisters expected a casual adventure. Instead, they encountered verglas—a thin glaze of ice on the rock—and a whiteout. They turned around at the Solvay Hut, an emergency shelter at 13,133 feet. At this point, they were roughly 2,440 vertical feet above the Hörnli Hut, where the climb begins, and still about 1,560 feet below the summit.

“It could be said I underestimated the Matterhorn myself in 2005,” Abegg told me. “Had we continued, it’s entirely possible we could have gotten into trouble.”

This past summer, Abegg returned, climbing the Hörnli Ridge with a partner before completing a solo, unsupported round trip from Zermatt in 10 hours, 8 minutes, and 19 seconds—the fastest women’s time then recorded on the FKT website, supported or unsupported. A month later, Kalie McCrystal lowered the record to 6 hours, 47 minutes, and 33 seconds.

The route’s moderate technical grade, fixed ropes, and popularity can make the Hörnli Ridge seem approachable. But finding the line and staying on solid rock demands attention. Stray from the standard route and the rock can become looser. Altitude, changing weather, and fall consequences add to the difficulty.

During Abegg’s partnered ascent this past summer, a washing-machine-sized boulder was accidentally dislodged. It tumbled down a gully, triggering what she described as a significant rockslide, mostly off route. Higher up, loose rock littered the climbing line. Abegg described rocks ranging in size from marbles to baseballs, or even volleyballs, that climbers could knock onto people below. The terrain, she said, had historically remained under snow year-round.

“Had to move very carefully,” she wrote. Guides stopped taking clients up the route during her trip.

Aside from the omnipresent risk of rockfall in any alpine environment, a 2025 study found that climate change has caused an increase in rockfall on the Matterhorn as permafrost thaws. Just a couple months ago, German online magazine Lacrux published an article about the increasing hazards of rockfall on the Matterhorn, as well as on Mont Blanc.

“Having the innate mountain sense to know when to call it is a valuable quality on an objective like this,” Abegg said.

Andy Hansen, an IFMGA-certified (International Federation of Mountain Guides) guide based in Longmont, Colorado, has guided clients on the Matterhorn twice. Speaking from his own experience, he strongly recommends hiring a guide for a first attempt.

He said recreational climbers in Western Europe are generally more accustomed to hiring guides than their counterparts in the United States. One advantage of hiring a guide on the Hörnli Ridge is how closely they follow variable conditions on a route, according to Hansen.

“The local guides have an intimacy with the mountain that gives them the advantage of having the route finding dialed, understanding the conditions of the mountain from day to day, and knowing where and when to move quickly to manage the rockfall hazard,” Hansen told me.

Hansen observed an unusual amount of rockfall in the Alps this past spring and summer, calling the Hörnli Ridge noticeably more unstable. He pointed to local guides’ familiarity with the ridge and their day-to-day knowledge of its conditions. A weather forecast can tell any climber how warm it’s likely to get, but knowing the ridge helps a guide judge which sections are most prone to rockfall, where to move quickly to limit exposure, and whether to climb that day at all.

However, whether a guide would have changed the outcome for Liner is an entirely different question. “It’s virtually impossible to say with any degree of certainty that had this party been with a mountain guide, the outcome would have been any different,” Hansen said. In his view, it was the kind of misfortune that could befall a guided party, too.

Hawkins told Climbing that they were aware of the risk of rockfall and had accepted it as a possible and uncontrollable hazard that you can’t “really do anything about.” He added that he never considered hiring a guide because he has sufficient experience and wants to take on alpine objectives independently. “If you do hire a guide, you didn’t climb the mountain,” he said of his philosophy.

While a guide is not required to climb the Matterhorn, it does materially improve your chances of reaching the summit. According to Global Summit Guide, an independent, research-based mountaineering resource based in Utah, the summit rate varies considerably depending on whether climbers are traveling with a guide.

A Global Summit Guide report updated this past July states that while the overall Matterhorn success rate is 55%, guided climbers see a 72% success rate, while unguided climbers hover around a 38% success rate. Meanwhile, first-timers like Liner and Hawkins only have an 18% shot at reaching the top. Furthermore, during the popular climbing season of May through October, October has the lowest success rate of 22%.

Global Summit Guide also reinforces the Matterhorn’s reputation as Europe’s most deadly mountain, with an average of eight to 12 fatalities annually. They note that about 1 in 140 climbers perish in their attempt to summit. More than 500 people (and counting) have died on the Matterhorn to date.

Dialogue and debate over the broader trends indirectly related to Liner’s death have already  emerged in the climbing community.

After Liner died, a Reddit thread in r/Mountaineering sparked debate about the climbing-related content he and Hawkins had posted on their Instagram accounts. “Obviously, there are videos of me and him partying in Europe, but when we’re actually climbing, I take precautions and I’m not an idiot when I climb,” Hawkins told Climbing. “I take safety as a number one precaution.” He added that Liner would “probably be laughing” at what Hawkins sees as misinformed comments online.

Then, in an Instagram reel posted on November 2, Washington-based gear manufacturer High Mountain Gear turned the discussion toward a different topic: a video Norwegian climber Magnus Midtbø made about his 2025 Matterhorn solo. High Mountain Gear took particular issue with Midtbø looking up how to use crampons shortly before his climb. In the comments of High Mountain Gear’s reel, some agreed that a climber with Midtbø’s reach ought to think about the example he sets. Others asked why he was being brought into a conversation about someone else’s accident.

Hawkins explained that he and Liner had set the Matterhorn as a big goal independent of any online content. “It’s just a climb we wanted to do for a long time,” Hawkins said of the Matterhorn. “It had nothing to do with any Instagram videos.” He noted that he wasn’t very familiar with Midtbø’s Matterhorn video.

Beyond this recent incident, when Midtbø’s video came out, Swiss public broadcaster SRF reported that Midtbø talked openly about his limited preparation. He struggled with the altitude and got off route. Other climbers had to call him back to the right line. Once he got down, he admitted he had underestimated the risk and urged viewers against following his example. Air Zermatt’s rescue chief Anjan Truffer told SRF that he worried viewers might still interpret Midtbø’s climb as a success, without appreciating the gap between his climbing ability and their own.

In Midtbø’s defense, however, he could have cut the moments when he was tired, lost, or scared. But he chose to leave them in. Some viewers in the YouTube comments took the climb as a cautionary tale. Others wanted a follow-up with a guide explaining where things nearly went wrong. Ultimately, given the irrelevance of Midtbø’s video to Hawkins’s and Liner’s Matterhorn objective, as well as the full disclosures that Midtbø provided in his video, the notion that YouTube content is to blame for this or any other fatality seems besides the point.

As a guide, Hansen sees responsibility on both sides of the screen. He said creators like Midtbø have some accountability for what they put out, even when they include a disclaimer. But viewers must assess whether their own skills match the demands of any climb described in online content.

Abegg’s father came home with a story about soloing the Matterhorn in a T-shirt. Abegg and her sister came home with a story about turning around at the Solvay Hut. Midtbø came home, too. But in his video, you can see how close he came to a different outcome when he lost the route on exposed terrain.

Kieran Liner didn’t come home. He was 20 years old. The mountain doesn’t care what drew you there, whose story you heard, or how long you spent preparing. Even the most experienced climber can be in the wrong place at the wrong time, especially when it comes to escalating hazards like rockfall.

Liner’s family is planning to celebrate his life in Pensacola and Austin. In her obituary, Newman invited everyone who knew him, shared his adventures, or found inspiration in his life to join them. “Whether you knew him for a lifetime or crossed paths with him only briefly,” she wrote, “you are part of the story he leaves behind.”

Climbing Magazine reached out to Kyle Willis of High Mountain Gear and Magnus Midtbø for comment, but have not received a response.

#8201. The 10 Best Gifts for Ultralight Hikers in 2026

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Alpenglow Gear Alpenflow Fuel Transfer Valve

Hoping to buy a gift for an ultralight hiker? Here’s the hard truth: Whatever you purchase will be weighed, then quietly stuffed in a closet. I know, because after a decade of thru-hiking, I’ve almost completely wallpapered my small room with all the copies of Wild I’ve been given. Thank you, but please stop.

Apart from heavy gifts, the last thing an ultralight hiker needs is someone else choosing their big three. The little things, though? That’s where a good gift can surprise them. This year’s picks tackle ten small annoyances of life on trail, from a rigid bottle that actually works with a filter to a sun glove that doesn’t plaster to your hands.

Single-use bottles crease, crinkle, and need replacing, but my original ThruBottle survived 1,800 miles this summer with plenty of life left. My only gripe was that it was too stiff to squeeze water through a filter. I’ve upgraded to the new ThruBottle 1000, which has a softer body and sheds nearly an ounce, weighing 2.2 ounces for a full liter.

The zip-lock bag you’d rather no one ever rummaged through has a 0.14-ounce alternative: this cap turns a compatible 28 mm bottle into a portable bidet. I find that it works best with a squeezable bottle. Unlike TP, it never runs out halfway through a section.

I sleep cold, and when the temperature drops on the trail, my ears and neck are often the first places I want extra warmth. The Shag Hood, made from Polartec Alpha Direct, covers them for 1.16 ounces, so I can skip carrying another full layer. Bonus: It’s gorpcore enough to wear off trail too.

My old half-finger sun gloves always came off inside out, and getting them back on over sweaty hands was a nightmare. The éclipse gloves have a thumb hole and mitten-style opening, so they slide on and off. They weigh 0.35 ounces and give me UPF 50+ sun protection on the backs of my hands, where multiple rounds of sunscreen have never been enough.

A camera buried in your pack takes no photos. The three-ounce Capture Clip attaches to a shoulder strap or belt, so I can grab my camera when the light is just right, instead of getting stuck crouching over my pack, still fumbling for it when the light’s gone.

The long handle keeps your knuckles out of dinner at the bottom of a freeze-dried meal bag. The 0.8-ounce titanium spork would outlast my hiking career if I could stop losing it. I found four on my last thru-hike, so I’m clearly not the only one.

A half-empty fuel canister is too precious to toss but annoying to carry. I’ve envied hikers using heavier transfer valves, but couldn’t justify the weight until the Alpenflow dropped. It weighs 0.09 ounces and transfers leftover fuel between two standard EN417 canisters, including those from MSR, Jetboil, and Snow Peak.

Leukotape is my holy grail bandage. It stays on through sweat, mud, and sketchy river crossings, and I’ve accidentally left a strip on for weeks. It’s gotten harder for me to find it in stores lately, so a spare roll is a keeper. I wrap a generous amount around my trekking poles instead of carrying the full 3.9-ounce roll.

For 10,000 thru-hiking miles, my pillow was the head of my dirty air mattress propped up on a water bottle, which rolled out from under me all night. Don’t make my mistake. For 1.9 ounces, the regular size is the real deal, and it packs down to the size of a pool ball. Pricey for a pillow, but I sleep better.

This 0.11-ounce Dyneema pouch stops loose tent stakes from rattling around in your pack. You don’t think you need one until a rogue stake starts working its way through your bug netting. Not that I, a seasoned professional and expert patcher, know anything about that.

Kate Hudson’s silver, bronze, and gold bow tree is a nostalgic Christmas look. Experts share how to get it right without it feeling dated.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's official; Kate Hudson’s Christmas tree from last year is still inspiring holiday decorations in 2026.

It's hardly a surprise. After all, the actress (best known for her starring turns in Bride Wars and How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days) kept her Christmas tree simple, classy, and very less is more: think silver, bronze and gold bows, a few ornaments and not much else.

Now, a bow is almost as Christmassy as it gets, whether it’s tied on a tree, a wreath or a present. A nostalgic tree does have one risk, though: if you do it without thinking it through, it can go from warm and charming to dated really quickly. Some experts gave me tips on how you can avoid this, and get Kate Hudson’s Christmas tree look.

For those who have yet to see Kate Hudson's Christmas tree in all its glory, flick your eyes downwards...

A post shared by Kate Hudson (@katehudson)

It feels like a rebellion against the minimalist matchy-matchy (and beige) trend that has been going on for so many years, doesn't it? “People are tired of the same old, store-bought, themed trees,” says Irena Cara, interior designer and co-founder of Nova Wrap.

Reilly Renwick, designer and creative lead of State of the Wall, points to Millennial parents whose kids are now the age they were in the 1990s. Many of them, he says, want to revive “the warm, festive and childlike vibe of a 90s Christmas, as opposed to what people are now calling the ‘sad beige’ of contemporary tree styling.”

So, how best to recreate it? Other than buying some of this beautiful metallic gold ribbon from Amazon. We have a few ideas...

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Hey, we might not have Goldie Hawn as a mum, but when it comes to Christmas nostalgia, a lot of millennials remember our parents' houses being packed with all kinds of stuff, and so much color that it felt cluttered. So, the biggest worry with going with a nostalgic look is the tree looking tacky.

For Renwick, “the biggest challenge for anyone trying to create a nostalgic tree is how to evade the ‘tacky’ accusations.” His answer is to look at what Kate Hudson did with hers. “The whole point of this ‘comeback’ thing is to evoke the festive vibe of the 90s, not to recreate it in painstaking detail,” he says.

Shop Nostalgic Christmas Tree Essentials:

Want the Kate Hudson look? “My advice is to use the metallic bows with restraint, in such a way that they stand out but still leave space for the other decorations and the tree itself to still be visible,” says Renwick.

Cara has practical tips for gold, silver, and bronze. “Use brushed or matte ribbon to take the ‘shiny’ edge off, especially if the metals are varying warm tones. Also, make sure the bows are of varying sizes, to keep things interesting.”

For quantity, she says: “On a tree between 6 and 7 feet, use between 20 and 30 bows.” Lighting matters too: “Warm white lights make metallics look even better.”

A Christmas tree runs the risk of feeling tacky, true, but it can also feel too generic, like it should be in a department store in the 90s. Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, has a way to avoid this.

“You can’t purchase nostalgia, but you can tie it!” she says. Her suggestion is to reuse ribbon that already means something. “Use ribbons that have a story, such as paper that a bouquet you received came wrapped in. On the loose end of the ribbon, write down the date you received it, and now your tree is a timeline.”

Melam preserves flowers for a living, so she also suggests pairing a ribbon with a flower from your own garden. She says you can build the look slowly: “You can add one more ribbon to your tree each year.”

If you already have tons of ornaments that have been passed down by family or maybe something your kids have made, bows can tie them into a whole scheme.

Cara says to put the old pieces where people look first: “Place heirloom and vintage pieces at eye level in the center where people look first.” Then, let the ribbon link everything together. “Match the ribbon to details on the older ornaments, such as a gold edge or a red glass.”

A big advantage of a bow tree like Kate Hudson's is that it’s very cheap to update, as ribbon is super easy to swap out for different colors and patterns. “Swap out the ribbon and keep the ornaments to change decorations year to year for a small cost,” says Cara.

Melam says to store ribbon carefully between seasons: “Moisture and light will cause your ribbon to fade, so store it flat in a cool, dark, dry place.”

Kate Hudson’s tree works because it feels warm and traditional without trying to look like a time capsule. Keep your color palette tight and give your ribbon some history to recreate the same nostalgia.

#8199. Iran Executed a Mountaineer for Alleged Violence in Anti-Government Protests. Hundreds More Face the Same Fate.

Ali Sina Mostafavi (Photo: Courtesy of Iran Human Rights)

Ali Sina Mostafavi dreamed of climbing Everest. In 2019, he trekked to its Base Camp. Under a photo of him pointing to the summit, he wrote on Instagram in English: “Top of the world. I promise to come back to you.”

Mostafavi never fulfilled his promise. On October 14, he was executed by the Iranian authorities in Kerman Central Prison.

The 38-year-old is one of at least 39 people to have been executed in connection with Iran’s anti-government protests last winter, and one of six athletes among them.

Dr. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, an ice climber and co-founder of the Norway-based Human Rights for Sport, told Climbing, “From a human rights perspective, every single aspect of this case is an absolute violation. The state has not made any credible, independently verifiable evidence public.”

Born in 1987 in Bam County, southeastern Iran, Mostafavi was a professional mountaineer and a member of the Speeco mountaineering club in his home city of Kerman. He called mountains ‘the love of his life,’ according to Abdollahkhani.

Mostafavi climbed two of Iran’s highest peaks, Damavand (5,610m/18,410ft) and Alam-Kuh (4,850m/15,910ft). In 2016, he ascended Mount Kazbek (5,054m/16,581ft) in Georgia.

In 2019, Mostafavi traveled to Nepal and summited Island Peak (6,189m/20,305ft) and trekked to Everest Base Camp. In 2022, he attempted Ama Dablam (6,812m/22,349ft), reaching 6,600m/21,654ft.

Mostafavi was married and had a 13-year-old daughter, Respina. Alongside his climbing career, he was an accomplished musician who played the tar, a traditional Persian lute. Friends spoke of his sensitive, artistic spirit, and his deep love for mountains, music, and animals—notably, his beloved cat and dog.

On his Instagram account, @everest_coldhell, his bio reads: ‘Mount Explorer. Love the nature. Musician.’

In December 2025, Iran’s economic crisis sparked street protests that developed into nationwide demonstrations against the Islamic Republic’s repressive regime, which enforces compulsory hijab laws restricting women’s autonomy, conducts violent crackdowns on protests, issues arbitrary arrests, and employs the use of torture.

In an attempt to suppress dissent, authorities used lethal force, killing thousands and arresting tens of thousands of protesters. The human rights organization Amnesty International called this “the deadliest period of repression by the Iranian authorities” in its decades of monitoring the country.

Following the assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei by US-Israeli airstrikes on February 28, Iran’s government intensified repressive crackdowns on dissent under the pretext of “wartime conditions.”

By October, at least 106 people arrested during the January protests had received death sentences, according to documentation by human rights organization Hengaw.

Iran carries out the world’s second-highest number of executions after China. In 2025, its government executed at least 2,159 people, the highest figure recorded by Amnesty International since 1981.

On Instagram, Mostafavi expressed support for Iran’s former Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, an exiled dissident who calls for a secular, democratic, and liberal Iran, describing him as “the only saviour of the homeland.” Two sources claim that Mostafavi’s family were set to move abroad before the 2022 ‘Woman, Life, Freedom’ protests began, but he ultimately chose to remain to fight for Iran’s future.

One obituary claims that he had been arrested twice in recent years for political activism and had spent time in Kerman Prison. This January, the mountaineer joined protests alongside millions of Iranians.

IranWire, an independent pro-democracy outlet, reported that Mostafavi was arrested three months later on April 25 alongside his wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé, while his mother’s home was also raided.

Mostafavi was reportedly beaten during his arrest and was forced to sign confession papers to release his family members. It is not known whether he had access to an independent lawyer, a right frequently denied to defendants in political and national security cases in Iran.

The Iranian judiciary’s account of the case was published by state-aligned media outlets including Mizan News Agency, Tasnim News Agency, the IRIB, and Tabnak. The allegations have not been independently verified.

The Judiciary of Iran claimed that Mostafavi had participated in the widespread anti-government protests in January, and that he was a member of the “Immortal Guards,” an armed wing of exiled dissident Reza Pahlavi’s group.

The judiciary also alleged that Mostafavi had shot and injured two civilians, fired at security forces, and possessed firearms, ammunition, and Molotov cocktails. It further accused him of communicating with foreign media and sharing footage of missile strike locations during the US-Iran war.

Mostafavi was convicted of the capital offense of moharebeh, or “enmity against God,” alongside several charges relating to alleged violence, weapons possession, and communication with hostile media. The evidence against him has not been made public.

The judiciary reported that the fiancé of Mostafavi’s sister received a prison sentence of 12 years and seven months for alleged cooperation, while he, his wife, and his sister were also sentenced to seven months in prison for posting content deemed as propaganda against the regime.

An appeal against Mostafavi’s death sentence was rejected. IranWire reported that he was transferred to solitary confinement the night before his execution and that family members were summoned. The judiciary announced that he was hanged at dawn in Kerman Central Prison on October 14. According to IranWire, Mostafavi asked the prison guards to pass along a message to the judge: “I did not wage war against God, nor did I commit moharebeh that you should charge me with it; my fight was with you.”

That evening, state-aligned outlet Tabnak published footage purporting to show Mostafavi’s arrest, weapons allegedly found in his possession, and a confession to a planned attack on Kerman Airport. IranWire reported that the confession appeared to have been made under duress and spliced together with unverified footage. Amnesty International has also identified signs of forced confessions in 18 videos of Iranian prisoners arrested between February and May 2026, during the same period as Mostafavi’s arrest.

Shortly after his death, a video of Mostafavi’s young daughter crying on her father’s grave, accompanied by their cat, circulated on social media.

Human rights groups have voiced concerns about Mostafavi’s case in the context of widespread forced confessions and sham trials lacking due process in Iran.

“The complete absence of forensic evidence or transparent court records confirms that his conviction rested entirely on forced confessions extracted under coercion rather than any objective proof,” Abdollahkhani said.

She explained that the arrest of Mostafavi’s wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé fits an established pattern of authorities using family members as leverage.

“The Islamic Republic routinely arrests close relatives and uses threats of torture or sexual violence to force athletes into making false confessions in a desperate bid to save their loved ones,” she said.

According to Human Rights for Sport, at least eight other mountaineers’ lives are at risk.

Maryam Hadavand Siri, a 42-year-old mother of two, led the Mountaineering Board of Pakdasht County in Tehran Province. She was arrested during the January protests, transferred to Evin Prison, and sentenced to death in April, without access to an independent lawyer. Following an appeal, her case was referred to the Supreme Court for review.

Social media activist and mountaineer Fatemeh Jami was arrested at her home on June 30 by Cyber Police officers. She was transferred to Gorgan Prison, where she remains detained without access to a lawyer or medical assistance.

Tara (Shirin) Masoudi, a member of the Razhan Mountaineering Group in Mahabad, was arrested on August 19. She was transferred to a detention centre and later released on bail. She is awaiting a final verdict.

Mohammad Hakimpour, Mostafa Ghaderi, Mohammad Saleh Hosseini, Hossein Abdollahi, and Khaled Rahimi—all members of climbing clubs in Saqqez—were arrested on October 8. According to Human Rights for Sport, they were subjected to physical abuse in detention and have been denied access to legal counsel, family visits, and telephone calls.

Abdollahkhani urges climbers to raise awareness of Mostafavi’s execution and the status of the eight other mountaineers, and to contact national federations, sports governing bodies, the International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation (UIAA), and the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

“How is it possible that a member of the climbing community is at risk of execution on alleged political charges, while the global climbing world stays silent?” she asked.

On October 30, Human Rights for Sport published an open letter to the UIAA executive board and athlete commission. In the letter, Abdollahkhani asks the UIAA to appeal directly to Iran’s national mountaineering federation, along with its Ministry of Sport and National Olympic Committee, to stop further executions and advocate for the release of imprisoned climbers.

Topo Athletic's new Traverse 2. (Photo: Topo Athletic)

It’s a toss-up what thru-hikers think about more: food, or their feet. After all, when you’re on the trail hour after hour, day after day, you can’t replenish calories fast enough. And at that pace, small flaws in shoe design can quickly magnify into a full-blown sufferfest. But with the right footwear—a shoe that provides the perfect combination of stability, durability, and comfort—thru-hikers can stop worrying about their feet and get on with daydreaming about their next cheeseburger.

Thru-hikers have already discovered Topo Athletic’s Traverse low-top hiking shoe, and appreciate its traction, toughness, and tailored fit on the longest trails. The latest iteration, the Traverse 2, builds on that foundation with new details geared specifically to multi-month objectives like the Appalachian Trail and Pacific Crest Trail.

Extended adventures demand durability, so the Traverse 2 features a new, high-abrasion mesh upper with strategically placed overlays that fend off trail debris without adding extra ounces (which is key when deciding what is and isn’t worth the weight on lengthy thru hikes). Protecting feet from dirt, rocks, and precipitation is also essential for logging long trail miles day after day, so Topo Athletic added its universal gaiter attachment system to the Traverse 2.

The Traverse 2 is built for anything the terrain throws at you. The full-length Vibram ® Megagrip outsole digs into technical, rocky, and wet trails, while a flexible forefoot rock plate beefs up underfoot protection. The three-piece midsole platform is designed for all-day hiking with a heavy pack, with a softer foam on the base of the heel and a firmer foam on the medial arch for maximum stability. Topo Athletic’s FKT insole features TPU beads not only for rebound and comfort, but also to help the shoes drain and dry in a flash. The shoe’s 5-millimeter drop hits the sweet spot to provide a more natural gait across long distances. And of course, the brand’s signature fit combines a roomy toe box with a snug fit around the midfoot and heel for a naturally comfortable feel.

All this comes in a streamlined package that keeps you light on your feet. The Traverse 2 weighs in at 9.2 ounces for a women’s 7 and 11.2 ounces for a men’s 9. It’s the kind of shoe that lets thru-hikers forget about their feet and focus on the adventure (or visions of that next cheeseburger).

Topo Athletic, based in Framingham, Massachusetts, empowers people to move better for life. Rooted in the belief that every step shapes the journey, Topo builds performance-driven footwear with a focus on lasting comfort and durability, all with its signature fit.

All-year backyard structure on a budget? Yes please! Evergreen shrubs are the landscape-design must every garden is missing, and these can all be planted now.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As leaves drop in fall, I always wish I’d planted more evergreen shrubs in my garden to give structure and color all through the winter. From tall arborvitae cones to slender columns of holly and perfect no-prune spheres, evergreens give a garden a shapely skeleton on which to hang seasonal blooms. While I’m lucky enough to have mature yew hedges and an old conifer I’m planning to cloud-prune, I want to add evergreen accents to borders and alongside a path to punctuate my garden design. Globes of green leaves in patio planters are high on my wish list too.

What's stopped me? One of the basic principles of garden design is to always repeat-plant evergreens in odd numbers – and bying multiple plants gets expensive, fast. But Home Depot must have been listening in to my garden-design dreams because it’s not even Thanksgiving yet and a heap of my favorite evergreen shrubs just had their prices slashed in an early Black Friday plant sale. And frankly, the prices were pretty decent even before they went on sale.

Let’s skip straight to the good bit, shall we?

While most boxwood shrubs grow incredibly slowly, sprinter boxwood lives up to its name, meaning you can buy a smaller, cheaper plant. And don’t worry that Buxus microphylla will grow too big because it maxes out at 2-4 feet high and wide: large enough to have an impact in your yard without taking over. Sprinter boxwood keeps its glossy green foliage year-round and has excellent resistance to diseases and pests, including boxwood blight. Suitable for zones 4-9, this handsome shrub is easily shaped to create structural evergreen mounds in a border, a low square hedge or appealing spheres in planters.

Thuja occidentalis ‘Anna van Vloten’ is a dwarf evergreen that naturally grows in a compact sphere without ever needing to be clipped. With wonderfully textural fan-like foliage, it keeps a bright golden-green tone year-round and grows well in zones 3-8. Anna’s Magic Ball arborvitae only grows to 10-15 inches high and wide and looks delightful dotted through a border. If you’re looking for compact shrubs to boost your curb appeal or want to add some stylish year-round planters to your patio, here’s the easy solution.

Here’s another dwarf cultivar of Thuja occidentalis that naturally grows in a compact ball shape without requiring any pruning. Danica America arborvitae is a little bigger at 2 feet high and wide and a brighter green, but what really sets it apart is its fan-like foliage that grows in vertical layers. The evergreen foliage is denser than Anna’s Magic Ball, too. Use it to create a smart geometric accent alongside a path or add stylish structure to a border without taking up too much space. It's one of the best evergreens for containers, too, and suitable for zones 3-7.

For instant style in zones 6-9, few evergreen shrubs have the striking aplomb of sky pencil holly. It’s a cultivar of the lovely Japanese holly and while it grows 6-10 feet tall, it stays a slender 1-2 feet wide with unusual vertical branches. The leaves are small, glossy and dark green – more like a boxwood than a holly – so the growth is dense, accentuating the shape. So, while sky pencil holly doesn’t boast red berries (though it does grow small black berries in fall), its silhouette provides more than enough drama. Happy in a large planter or in well-drained ground, sky pencil holly looks fabulous either side of a doorway or gate, or planted in a loose line, and is one of the best shrubs for a front yard.

So far, so green. And while it’s wonderful to have shrubs that bring texture and a year-round skeleton of leaves, some evergreen shrubs also deliver a generous splash of color. And Encore azalea is one of the very best flowering plants to add to your garden in fall. While many azaleas are deciduous, and older varieties only flower for a few short weeks in spring, the Encore series not only keeps its leaves through winter but repeat-blooms all through spring, summer and autumn. It maintains a tidy, rounded shape so requires very little pruning, and there are all sorts of flower colors to choose from. Suitable for zones 6-10, Autumn Royalty has bright magenta blooms and you’ll also find Autumn Lily with white flowers, Autumn Carnation with pink flowers, and Autumn Embers with red-orange flowers in Home Depot’s sale.

Euonymus fortunei ‘Roemertwo’ is one of those easy wins that every garden needs, requiring little looking after but working hard four seasons of the year. Don't be put off by the fact it's a wintercreeper as this cultivar is a compact mounding shrub. Its evergreen foliage doesn’t lose its variegation and revert to green like many shrubs, and thank goodness because the lime-green leaves have lovely gold margins that positively glow on a dark winter day. Adding to the color, Gold Splash wintercreeper boasts yellow fruit that open to reveal orange seeds in fall. Highly resistant to disease, this neat, ultra-tough shrub reaches 18-24 inches high and wide in zones 5-8.

Okay, so Viburnum nudum ‘Brandywine’ isn’t evergreen but it does look good all through winter on account of the multi-colored berries that cling to the branches months after leaves have fallen. Brandywine viburnum is one of the best berry-bearing shrubs to feel birds through winter as its berries only sweeten once the worst winter weather sets in, providing a valuable late-season pantry for our feathered friends. Those berries provide quite a show, too, starting green then shifting through pink and blue to a glossy dark purple. Hardy in zones 5-9, this low-maintenance shrub reaches 5-6 feet high.

#8191. This New Book Strives to Help Climbers Rewire Their Mental Game

(Photo: Left: Sam Douglas Jones / Right: Vertebrate Publishing)

We all do it: Eyeing other climbers and comparing ourselves to them. Wishing we were better at dynos, heel hooks, or some other elusive climbing move. Loading ourselves with shoulds when it comes to training or grades.

Even non-performance-oriented climbers like me tend to be guilty of at least some negative thoughts when we’re up on the wall. It’s hard not to think that way when so many highly specific levels dominate the sport. This makes the idea of progression almost impossible to resist, even if you claim to do it only for fun.

There is something about the progress ladder of the Yosemite Decimal System. Its slash grades, letter addendums, and pluses and minuses tempt you to try and tick routes with higher grades. The same goes for the V-scale, as well as many other grading scales. We often ask “What if?” questions about breaking into a harder grade. And we often define ourselves by the grades we climb. “I’m a V10 boulderer,” someone might say, or “I’m a 5.10 climber.”

Meanwhile, when I’m skiing or mountain biking, there are essentially only four, color-coded levels, green through double black. Compared to climbing, I find it rare for someone to ask what color run I skied or trail I rode—and did I make it down without falling? But after someone climbs a route, one of the first questions might be what the grade was. And did you send it?

As the sport continues to grow, two British climbers have noticed that the expansion of training content has far outpaced the rise of mindset content when it comes to climbing. And they agree that climbing tends to be uniquely progress-oriented compared to other sports.

“It’s great to see the growth in top-end performance climbing, but for a lot of people, that might come with a lot of pressure to perform the same way,” says Louis Parkinson, the founder of the coaching company Catalyst Climbing, a climber of over 20 years, and co-author of the new book Get a Grip.

To write a self-help book for climbers focused exclusively on mindset, Parkinson teamed up with Joel Robertson, an MA MBACP psychotherapist and climber. Nicknamed “The Climbing Therapist,” Robertson insists that their book isn’t only for elite or performance-oriented athletes. That’s because he believes climbers at any level can experience the pressure and negative thought patterns that the sport can induce. He also sees negative mentality extending beyond the sport.

“If you’re being brutal to yourself at the crag or in the gym in ways that are holding you back in climbing, then you’re almost certainly doing that to yourself at family Christmas or at work or whatever,” Robertson says. “Mental health and climbing mindset are not separate, right? Let’s treat them the same. That’s the whole ethos of the book.”

Both Parkinson and Robertson admit that they are far from perfect when it comes to their own mentality. They emphasize that a healthy climbing mindset requires continuous work, rather than a one-time solution.

A former competitive climber, Parkinson recalls a period where he stopped enjoying climbing. This triggered an identity crisis of sorts, since he had oriented his entire life and career around the sport. “If I stop climbing, then I don’t know who I am,” Parkinson recalls thinking.

Eventually, Parkinson realized that his lack of enjoyment stemmed from the immense pressure he was putting on himself to continuously improve. When he couldn’t perform up to his own standards, he became “really, really upset.” Once he eased off the unrealistic expectations he was holding himself too, the joy came back. Parkinson’s past struggle echoes a similar experience of Chris Sharma. Earlier this year, he talked with Climbing about letting go of grades in order to send Biographie, the world’s first 5.15.

Robertson, primarily a casual indoor boulderer, shares a more recent experience from a couple weeks ago. After three sessions, he flashed his gym project. In the midst of some celebratory fist pumps, however, he watched in mild horror as someone else came and flashed his project as their warm-up. “It’s so classic,” Robertson says of this common climbing predicament. “I genuinely felt way less good about the achievement and not just the achievement, but myself.”

To avoid comparing yourself to others in a negative way, one suggestion Get a Grip offers is to think about your climbing friends. Do you love and value them because of their climbing ability, or because of who they are? Most people care about each of their friends as a person, not in terms of their climbing abilities. When you start to compare yourself to others, or base your self-worth on whether you, for example, sent your project, try to view yourself as you would your friend instead.

Robertson and Parkinson also suggest focusing on comparisons that are accurate and valuable, rather than grounded in envy or self-pity. Instead of thinking, “Damn, I wish I could climb like that,” ask, “What could I learn from watching someone else that I could apply in my own climbing?”

One of the critical ways to work on climbing mindset is to cultivate more awareness around our own thoughts, according to Robertson and Parkinson. Rather than becoming bogged down in the thought, attempt to view the thought impartially. Try reframing the thought, or compartmentalizing it. “Rather than ‘I am anxious,’ it’s ‘a part of me is anxious,’” Robertson explains. This can help you get some distance between yourself and a fleeting notion or emotion.

Throughout the book, reflections from pro climbers bring more color and insight to what a strong mindset looks like. In one of my favorite sections, British boulderer and competitive climber Shauna Coxsey talks about asking questions instead of making statements. An “exploratory mindset,” as Robertson and Parkinson term it, will fuel you with curiosity rather than pressure. “People often think I’m a very motivated person, but I would disagree,” Coxsey writes after sharing her focus on curiosity. “I think I’m a very committed person. For me, motivation and commitment have to go hand in hand because it’s impossible to be motivated all the time.”

Another standout pro mindset cameo comes from another British boulderer and comp climber: Hamish McArthur. Essentially, he reveals that he more or less blacks out when he climbs hard. This allows him to enter the coveted flow state that so many of us seek. “The times when I’ve performed at my best, I don’t really have any memory of what it was like,” he writes.

I took a lot away from the book in terms of how to edit and take control of my internal monologue. But I was left with one nagging question: How can we all climb more like McArthur, and find that elusive flow state?

“Just think less. It’s easy!” Parkinson joked with me. “No, it’s really hard. It’s insanely difficult.” Parkinson clarifies that achieving a mindset like McArthur’s requires a long-term commitment to honing your meditation skills so you can quiet your mind and just climb. But the lessons in Get a Grip can help get you started.

Vertebrate Publishing released Get a Grip on October 8. You can find a copy from Catalyst Climbing, Amazon, and wherever books are sold. Climbers can also listen to Get a Grip as an audiobook narrated by Parkinson.
